title: NG2: Infiniteness (Prop 1) not proven for general odd c -- internal-internal geodeticity only checked c<=11

comments.author: critic-agent
comments.body:
**Location:** solution.tex, Proposition 1 (Uniform odd scalings), lines 205-233.

**The gap.** The proof rigorously establishes only the BRANCH-source condition (I), via the parity argument 2s=c*k, k in {0,1,2}, impossible for odd c (lines 217-224). The remaining INTERNAL-INTERNAL instances of (G) -- precisely the obstruction the solution elsewhere insists is the hard, global one (Remark, lines 184-201) -- are dismissed in one sentence: "verified directly (check.py) for the fixed structure of H," with brute force only "for all odd c<=11" (lines 225-230). No argument valid for ALL odd c is given.

**Why this is non-trivial.** For p on e=ab (offset r) and q on f=cd (offset s), d_{G}(p,q) = min over the four endpoint choices of (offset) + c*d_H(.,.) + (offset). Ties such as r+s=c are arithmetically available for odd c (e.g. c=3, r=1, s=2); they are broken only because some THIRD route (via a common neighbour, e.g. d with d_H(a,d)=1) strictly undercuts. That is a fact about the metric of H, not about parity. A complete proof must show, for every odd c, that no internal-internal tie survives -- i.e. identify the structural property of H (diameter-2 / girth-5 / Moore: any two vertices at distance 2 have a unique common neighbour) that guarantees it.

**Why load-bearing.** Infiniteness is the entire basis of Corollary 1 ("ill-posed; no finite exact count"), the solution principal rebuttal to the problem exact-count demand. If geodeticity of uniform odd c fails for some large c, the solution set could be finite and the problem premise vindicated. Related to the carried-over finiteness gap G3 (rm-05346-4), but here the issue is the OPPOSITE claim (infiniteness) being under-proven.

**To close.** Prove, c-independently, that whenever two endpoint choices tie for d_{G}(p,q) in the uniform-c subdivision, a third choice using a common neighbour is strictly smaller. The Moore uniqueness of common neighbours should make this clean.

comments.author: critic-agent
comments.body:
**Update for the current (revised) solution.tex — the gap persists with a precise new location.**

The revision replaced the old "check.py for $c\le 11$" with a full analytic argument (lines 305–330). However the argument contains a concrete error at the decisive internal–internal sub-case, so NG2 is **not** closed.

**Where.** Line 328: "*The value $0$ forces $n_a=n_b$ **and** $c-2t=0$ (impossible, $c$ odd)*."

**Why it is wrong.** For $p$ on $e=ab$ (offset $r$, and we are in the reduced case $r=t$) and $q$ internal on $f=\{c_0,d_0\}$ (offset $t$), write the realizing sides $d(a,q)=c\,n_a+t_a$, $d(b,q)=c\,n_b+t_b$ with $(n_\bullet,t_\bullet)\in\{(n(\cdot,c_0),t),(n(\cdot,d_0),c-t)\}$. Then
$$\mathrm{diff}=d(a,q)-d(b,q)=c(n_a-n_b)+(t_a-t_b),\qquad t_a\ne t_b\Rightarrow t_a-t_b=\pm(2t-c)=\mp(c-2t).$$
Setting $\mathrm{diff}=c-2t$ (the bad tie, since $r=t$) gives $c(n_a-n_b)=(1\pm1)(c-2t)\in\{0,\,2(c-2t)\}$. The branch $c(n_a-n_b)=0$ forces **only** $n_a=n_b$; it imposes **no** constraint on $t$. When $n_a=n_b$ — i.e. $a$ enters $f$ via $d_0$ and $b$ via $c_0$ with $n(a,d_0)=n(b,c_0)$ — the equation is an **identity**, so $\mathrm{diff}=c-2t=c-2r$ genuinely holds: an **actual (G)-tie**, exactly the internal–internal obstruction this issue is about. The text's "$c-2t=0$" is unjustified.

**What is actually needed (as this issue originally said).** The tie is broken only because the offending two sides are **not the true simultaneous minima**: a third route through the **common neighbour** (Moore: a distance-2 pair of branch vertices has a *unique* common neighbour; adjacent endpoints use girth 5) strictly undercuts $d_{G'}(p,q)$. That is a metric fact about $H$, invisible to the residue-mod-$c$ / $n_\bullet\in\{0,1,2\}$ bookkeeping the revised proof uses.

**To close.** Prove the common-neighbour undercut lemma: whenever two endpoint-entry choices tie for $d_{G'}(p,q)$ in the uniform-$c$ subdivision, routing through the (unique) common neighbour gives a strictly shorter walk, so no tie is a true geodesic tie. This is c-independent and kills the $n_a=n_b$ identity sub-case. Until then Proposition 1 — and hence Corollary 1's infiniteness/ill-posedness verdict — is unproven.
